# Phase 22: a faster snapshot restore

[Phase 20](PHASE_20.md) found that a session restore was about half disk read and half rebuild,
the two running one after the other, and named a fix it did not build. This phase builds it and
measures both paths in one process. Questions were fixed in `configs/phase22.yaml` before any run.

## What was built

- **`TieredLayer.from_store`** (`lazykv/tiered.py`): a layer whose pinned host store already holds
  its sealed blocks. It brings the store to the GPU in chunks of 256 blocks, derives the Quest
  metadata and the seeded slots from them, and writes the sink and the unsealed tail, all queued
  without a host sync. The constructor (the prefill boundary) derives the same things from the same
  bytes, so the two build equal layers; it is refactored so both share the allocation and the
  residency table.
- **`snapshot.restore(rebuild="store")`**, now the default, reads each tiered layer's blocks
  straight into its pinned host store and calls `from_store`. Because nothing waits for the GPU, a
  layer's copies and metadata run while the next layer is read from disk; one sync at the end.
  `rebuild="boundary"` keeps Phase 20's path: read into pageable memory, copy to the GPU, hand the
  layer to the constructor, which copies it back to the host store.
- Tests (`tests/test_snapshot.py`): a layer from `from_store` equals the constructor's in every
  tensor and table, with and without a tail, with spare slots, and across chunk edges; restored
  tiny-model sessions continue bit-identically under both paths, buffered and unbuffered.

Phase 20 kept the boundary path on purpose, because reusing it made a restore provably a prefill.
The store path gives that up for a test and a hash: it is checked, not shared.

## The run

Phase 20's setup unchanged: Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, one NIAH prompt per context, the speed kernel,
the tier at a 12.5% budget, the snapshot on the internal NVMe (C:),
every read unbuffered. Per context, 3 tiered prefills, then
3 restores per path, the two paths interleaved and their order
alternating between repeats.

### Questions 1 and 2: cost, and what is left

| Context | Rebuild | Restore (median, range) | In reads | Outside reads (share) | Snapshot bytes / restore time | Transient VRAM, max | Over tiered prefill (its median) | State hash equal |
| --: | --- | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| 32,768 | Store (this phase) | 0.37 s (0.36–0.51) | 0.31 s | 0.05 s (13%) | 2.87 GB/s | 120 MiB | 15.3× (5.72 s) | 3 / 3 |
| 32,768 | Boundary (Phase 20) | 0.59 s (0.59–0.60) | 0.33 s | 0.26 s (43%) | 1.82 GB/s | 248 MiB | 9.7× (5.72 s) | 3 / 3 |
| 65,536 | Store (this phase) | 0.75 s (0.75–0.95) | 0.66 s | 0.08 s (11%) | 2.85 GB/s | 176 MiB | 23.8× (17.91 s) | 3 / 3 |
| 65,536 | Boundary (Phase 20) | 1.17 s (1.16–1.18) | 0.66 s | 0.50 s (43%) | 1.83 GB/s | 496 MiB | 15.3× (17.91 s) | 3 / 3 |
| 130,048 | Store (this phase) | 1.37 s (1.35–1.47) | 1.18 s | 0.15 s (11%) | 3.12 GB/s | 286 MiB | 44.2× (60.51 s) | 3 / 3 |
| 130,048 | Boundary (Phase 20) | 2.14 s (2.13–2.18) | 1.14 s | 1.00 s (47%) | 1.99 GB/s | 984 MiB | 28.3× (60.51 s) | 3 / 3 |

| Context | Store over boundary (medians) | Worst pairing (slowest store, fastest boundary) |
| --: | --: | --: |
| 32,768 | 1.57× | 1.16× |
| 65,536 | 1.56× | 1.22× |
| 130,048 | 1.56× | 1.45× |

- **The store path restores 1.56× to
  1.57× faster than the boundary path** at the
  medians, at every context. Pairing the slowest store restore with the fastest boundary one, it is
  still 1.16× faster.
- **A restore is now mostly the disk.** Under the store path,
  11%–13%
  of the wall time is spent outside reads, against
  43%–47%
  under the boundary path. The read itself costs the same on both paths: it was already reading at
  the disk's rate, and the store path only changed where the bytes land.
- **Resuming is now 15.3× to
  44.2× faster than prefilling again**
  (prefill re-measured in this run; the boundary path gives
  9.7× to
  28.3×).
- What remains outside reads is the last layer's GPU work, which has no next read to hide behind,
  and the two dense layers, which are still restored as Phase 20 did. Faster from here means a
  faster disk or reading while the previous read's bytes are still being copied, not more overlap.

### Question 3: exactness

- **Every restore is exact.** The full tier state hash matched the prefilled tier's on
  18 of 18 restores,
  both paths. Decoded tokens matched on 15 of
  18; with identical state, the mismatches are cuDNN's
  single-query decode, which is not bit-repeatable (Phase 1), as the config said before the run.

### Question 4: transient VRAM

- **The store path's peak above the restored tier is
  286 MiB at most, against
  984 MiB for the boundary path.**
  The config expected one 256-block chunk (32 MiB on this model). It is more, and it grows with
  context, because the dense layers are still restored by copying a whole layer's KV to the GPU at
  once; at the longest context the peak is that copy plus one chunk. The tiered layers' part is the
  chunk, as expected. Restoring the dense layers in chunks too would remove the rest; not built.

## What this phase does not show

- One model, one prompt per context, one disk. A slower disk makes reads a larger share, which
  favours neither path more; the absolute saving is the boundary path's rebuild.
- Restores into pools pinned in advance, as in Phase 20. A cold process pays the pinning once.
- No session was resumed mid-conversation in this run; the unit tests cover splits after decoding.
